## Advanced reactors are where the fixed event tree is weakest {#why-dynamic data-section="1"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.9em;"}
- **Passive safety**: success is the outcome of a thermal-hydraulic
  trajectory, not a component state
- **Sparse operating experience**: little history from which to fix the
  sequences in advance
- **New operating concepts**: reduced staffing, remote supervision,
  autonomous control
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.9em;"}
Risk-informed, performance-based licensing asks for defensible coverage of
sequences and uncertainties, [not a handful of bounding
scenarios.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
[**Classical PRA**: structure and timing are fixed before any computation.]{style="font-size:0.74em; display:block;"}

![](figs/tikz/classical-et.svg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

[**Dynamic PRA**: the tree grows while a simulator runs; plant, crew and hardware co-evolve, and the sequences are an *output*.]{style="font-size:0.74em; display:block; margin-top:0.7em;"}

![](figs/tikz/dpra-tree.svg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::
::::

::: {.slideref}
NEI 18-04, Rev. 1 (2019); NRC Regulatory Guide 1.233 (2020); Aldemir, *Ann. Nucl. Energy* **52** (2013).
:::

::: {.notes}
Why do advanced reactors need dynamic PRA? A classical PRA fixes the accident
sequences before any computation: the analyst draws the event tree, and timing
enters only through success criteria and human error probabilities.

That is weakest exactly where advanced reactors differ from the operating
fleet. Passive safety is not a component that works or fails; its success is
the outcome of a thermal-hydraulic transient. There is little operating
experience to fix the sequences in advance. And the operating concepts are
new: reduced staffing, remote supervision, autonomous control.

Dynamic PRA grows the tree while a simulator runs, so the sequences are an
output of the analysis, not an input.
:::

## How a dynamic event tree is built {#anim-det data-section="1" background-iframe="assets/anim/det-animation.html" background-interactive="true" visibility="uncounted" .no-band}

::: {.notes}
[Animation. It starts by itself, runs about thirty-eight seconds and stops on
its last picture. Start reading as soon as it appears, and move on when you
have finished the text. The slide PDF shows the last picture only; the text is
the same.]

Here is how such a tree is built. A plant simulation starts at the initiating
event, on the left. At every pivotal event, marked with a flag, the full state
is saved, and one branch starts for each possible outcome: a component fails
or holds, the crew acts early or late. Between the flags it is deterministic
physics.

Each branch carries a conditional probability, and the sequences end at
different times, in different end states. The tree is the output. And every
pivotal event is a record: the time, the saved state, the trigger, and each
alternative with its probability.
:::

## Two barriers to routine dynamic PRA {#two-barriers data-section="1"}

```{=html}
<div class="xcards">
  <div class="xcard">
    <div class="x-name">Monolithic coupling</div>
    <div class="x-how">The engine is welded to one physics code, in one process. Retargeting it to the physics of an advanced reactor means merging code.</div>
    <div class="x-big">1 code</div>
    <div class="x-cap">RELAP5/MOD3.3 was the only physics ADS-IDAC could drive, built with one compiler on one workstation</div>
  </div>
  <div class="xcard">
    <div class="x-name">Combinatorial growth</div>
    <div class="x-how">Every branch point multiplies the sequences, and every sequence is a full transient. A study of realistic scope is compute-bound.</div>
    <div class="x-big">10<sup>4</sup> to 10<sup>5</sup></div>
    <div class="x-cap">simulations, perhaps more: a proper dynamic PRA takes tens to hundreds of thousands of full transients, and the original engine ran them one at a time</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
**ADS-IDAC** couples RELAP5, the IDAC crew cognitive model and hardware
reliability, and it showed both barriers.
[This talk: the two architectural moves that remove them, and what they
measurably buy.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::

::: {.slideref}
ADS-IDAC: Coyne and Mosleh, *Int. J. Performability Eng.* **10** (2014). IDAC: Chang and Mosleh, *Reliab. Eng. Syst. Saf.* **92** (2007).
:::

::: {.notes}
If the method fits this well, why is it not in routine use? The method is more
than twenty years old, and what held it back is tooling. Two barriers keep
coming back.

The first is monolithic coupling: the engine is welded to one physics code, in
one process, so moving it to the physics of an advanced reactor means merging
code.

The second is combinatorial growth: every branch point multiplies the
sequences, and each sequence is a full transient. A proper dynamic PRA takes
tens to hundreds of thousands of simulations, perhaps more.

ADS-IDAC, which couples RELAP5, the IDAC crew model, and hardware reliability,
had both: one physics code, and one sequence at a time.
:::

## Two moves that remove the barriers {#two-moves data-section="1"}

```{=html}
<div class="cols3">
  <div class="col c2">
    <div class="k">Move 1</div>
    <div class="h">Physics becomes a service</div>
    <ul>
      <li>the PRA core (time, branching, the crew model) is separated from plant physics</li>
      <li>a documented HTTP/REST contract of six endpoints</li>
      <li>a new code, a surrogate or a digital twin couples by implementing endpoints, not by merging code</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
  <div class="col c3">
    <div class="k">Move 2</div>
    <div class="h">The tree is traversed in parallel</div>
    <ul>
      <li>an MPI server and workers</li>
      <li>the server handles metadata only</li>
      <li>restart state travels worker to worker; LZ4 compression keeps it small</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
  <div class="col c5">
    <div class="k">Evidence</div>
    <div class="h">Demonstrated and measured</div>
    <ul>
      <li>a browser workflow with no MPI and no Fortran</li>
      <li>one contract, a PWR and a space fission reactor</li>
      <li>measured speedups, from a workstation to a cluster</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="band-note"><code>checkpoint()</code> and <code>restore()</code>: one primitive under all of it. It gives branching, distribution across workers, and whole-study fault tolerance.</div>
```

::: {.notes}
So the work is two moves, one for each barrier.

The first move separates the PRA core, meaning time advancement, branching,
and the crew model, from the plant physics. Physics becomes a service behind a
documented interface. The second move traverses the tree in parallel.

Both rest on one primitive, checkpoint and restore: save the complete state of
a simulation, and bring it back to life somewhere else.

I will take the two moves in turn, and then show the evidence.
:::
